Hi, just emailed this questions to the he...@r-inla.org, but I think this is a publicly interesting questions

B:  Spatial and Spatio-Temporal models with R-INLA. M Blangiardo, M Cameletti, G Baio, H Rue - Spatial and Spatio-temporal Epidemiology, 2013 - Elsevier

Sorry. I think I was vague.
A feature of any funtion in R that takes a formula in the standard way (inla, lm, glm etc) is that it automatically fits an intercept.

If you *do not* want to fit an intercept, you have to specifically tell R.

A BYM model with an intercept is
Y~f(region.struct,model="bym",graph.file="germany.graph")
Or
Y~1+f(region.struct,model="bym",graph.file="germany.graph")
(These are equivalent)

A BYM model without an intercept (and, as win bugs says, this is not a good model to fit) is Y~ -1 + f(region.struct,model="bym",graph.file="germany.graph")

The "-1" term says "don't fit an intercept".

I find it helps a lot to start by writing the desired model on
mathematical form instead of starting with an R formula; "a

> form = counts~1+f(ID,model="besag", graph.file = g)+f(inla.group(ID),

I assume that you really meant inla.group(temporal.ID), so that ID
contains graph node indices and temporal.ID contains temporal indices or
timepoints?
In that case the above gives a model

   eta_ij = beta_0 + x_i + z_j
   counts_ij ~ ZIP(eta_ij)

where x_i is a spatial/graph model and z_j is a temporal AR model.
If what you really want is a full space-time interaction model, i.e. you
want

   eta_ij = beta_0 + x_ij

then that can be obtained in the same way as for spde space-time models,
e.g. something like this:

form = counts~1+f(ID,model="besag", graph.file = g,
group=inla.group(temporal.ID), control.group=list(model="ar1"))

This is a general property of linear models, and not specific to R-INLA,
but basically this is the situation:

For any covariate with values x_i, any model of the form
   a + x_i*b
can be rewritten as
   (a+m*b) + (x_i-m)*b
where m is an arbitrary constant, reparameterised into
   alpha + z_i*b
where z_i is a shifted version of the covariate.
Note that the structure of the model did not change, but the values of
the a and alpha parameters are not the same, but they are related via
the value of m and the b parameter.
It is common to center the x_i covariate by choosing m=mean(x_i) (or
some other value that will act as the new "origin" for the covariate),
since this makes alpha and b less correlated than a and b would be, in
the posterior distribution, and it also improves the numerical
properties of the model.  When doing a fully Bayesian analysis with
vague priors on the parameters the difference is in theory small, but in
practice centering can be useful.  E.g., due to the reduced correlation,
the posterior marginal distributions for alpha and b are intuitively
easier to interpret than the posterior marginals for a and b.

This should be covered in any decent textbook on linear models (the
frequentistic version of these models tend to use centering even more
than Bayesian methods, so there should be plenty to read).  One just
needs to keep in mind what the interpretation of the intercept parameter
(a and alpha, respectively) is in the different models.

In your case, I'd suggest replacing 2000,2001,2002 by -1,0,1, so that
the intercept parameter becomes the average effect over the three years
(with 1,2,3 instead of -1,0,1 the intercept would try to capture the
effect for year 1999, which is a bit odd in terms of interpretation...)

Finn L

The cpo values are computed from the posterior density of the linear
predictor eta[i] without the contribution from the i'th datapoint y[i].
They way that it is computed, assumes that for the posterior density for
eta[i] with all the data and without  y[i], does not change to much. If

situation. So internally, this is checked for and if the conditions are

are not compute, and are simply set to 0 (I think). there is a function
'inla.cpo' that can be used to compute the 'failure' ones 'manually'.
There is also a question if we could approximate these in another way
using just Gaussians...

On 31 Jul 2013, at 09:34, Linh Nguyen <linh.vaw...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Dear All,
>
> I am thinking how to calculate a precision matrix in a spatial model.
> For example, in Gaussian Process, we can calculate a covariance matrix of unobserved locations, given observations.
> Equivalently, can we compute such precision matrix in Gaussian Markov Random Field?

When working with precision matrices and spatial models, things are done a bit differently than when working with covariance matrices.  I r-inla, the precision for the basis weights in a spatial spde model can be obtained from inla.spde.precision().  Calling that precision Qx, a linear Gaussian model with observation model y_i=(A x)_i + epsilon_i can be written as

X~N(mu, Qx)
Y|X=x ~ N(A x, Qeps)

The posterior distribution for X given Y=y is then given by

X|Y=y ~ N(mupost, Qpost)

Where

Qpost = Qx + A' Qeps A
mupost = mu + Qpost^-1 A' Qeps (y - A mu)

The basis weights in mupost can then be used to evaluate the posterior mean at any location of the field.  (The standard deviations require a bit more work and I don't have time to write all that in this email...)

All of this happens internally in r-inla and so it's not usually something one needs to do manually (except possibly when predicting onto more locations than inla can handle simultaneously)

So this only partially answered your question.  Other versions of the answer depends on _why_ you would want to have that precision matrix!

Finn
